top_level_objectives: Describe the observed pattern of Mars’s apparent retrograde motion against the background stars.
Explain why geocentric models required epicycles to reproduce retrograde loops.
Use a heliocentric perspective to connect retrograde motion to Earth overtaking Mars in its orbit.
Compare the size and timing of retrograde loops for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn based on orbital distance and relative motion.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the observable phenomenon from an Earth-based perspective before explaining its cause.
key_visuals: A dark sky dome with background constellations and a highlighted ecliptic path.
Mars marked as a bright reddish point with date labels appearing night by night.
A faint trail showing Mars first drifting eastward among the stars.
student_actions: Advance time in one-week steps and observe Mars’s position relative to nearby stars.
Place markers at several dates to build the apparent path.
Identify the normal eastward drift before the reversal begins.

scenes.brief_purpose: Focus attention on the reversal, loop, and return to prograde motion as the central puzzle.
key_visuals: Mars’s full multi-month track drawn over the constellations, including a westward loop.
Color-coded segments for prograde, slowing/stationary, retrograde, and resumed prograde motion.
Labels for eastern drift, western reversal, and stationary points.
student_actions: Scrub through the event night by night and note when Mars appears to slow, stop, reverse, and stop again.
Trace the loop with a finger or controller and label the retrograde segment.
Answer a short prompt describing what makes the motion surprising.

scenes.brief_purpose: Show why retrograde motion was difficult to explain in an Earth-centered model and motivate epicycles.
key_visuals: Earth fixed at the center with the Sun, stars, and Mars arranged in a simplified geocentric diagram.
A simple circular path for Mars failing to match the observed loop.
An added epicycle-on-deferent path that can reproduce a loop but looks mechanically complex.
student_actions: Compare the observed sky track with the prediction from a simple geocentric circle.
Toggle an epicycle model on and off to see how the loop can be fitted.
Reflect on why adding epicycles made the model more complicated.

scenes.brief_purpose: Shift to an outside-the-solar-system view where Earth and Mars move smoothly around the Sun.
key_visuals: A scaled schematic of the Sun at the center with circular or slightly elliptical orbits for Earth and Mars.
Earth moving faster on the inner orbit and Mars moving slower on the outer orbit.
A line of sight from Earth to Mars projected outward onto a distant star background.
student_actions: Run the orbital animation and compare Earth’s and Mars’s speeds.
Pause at several dates and inspect the Earth-Mars line of sight.
Connect the projected line of sight to Mars’s apparent position on the star background.

scenes.brief_purpose: Make the causal mechanism explicit: retrograde motion occurs as Earth passes Mars on the inside track.
key_visuals: Earth approaching, aligning with, and passing Mars near opposition.
Successive Earth-Mars sight lines fanning across the distant star sphere.
A synchronized inset showing the same dates as a sky-view loop.
student_actions: Step through the overtaking sequence and watch how the sight line shifts backward against the stars.
Match orbital positions to the prograde, stationary, and retrograde parts of the sky track.
Use a short car-passing analogy prompt to explain the apparent backward motion.

scenes.brief_purpose: Generalize the explanation and show why more distant outer planets have less dramatic loops.
key_visuals: Three selectable outer planets—Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn—on increasingly large orbits.
Side-by-side sky tracks showing different retrograde loop sizes and durations.
Indicators for orbital distance, orbital speed, and relative motion compared with Earth.
student_actions: Select Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn and run the same Earth-overtaking visualization for each.
Compare the apparent loop width and rate of motion for the three planets.
Explain why Jupiter and Saturn show smaller, slower retrograde shifts than Mars.

scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate the observational and heliocentric perspectives into a coherent explanation.
key_visuals: A split view with the Earth-sky retrograde loop on one side and the heliocentric orbit diagram on the other.
Linked date markers showing the same moments in both views.
A concise summary diagram: prograde motion, opposition/overtaking, retrograde interval, return to prograde.
student_actions: Arrange event cards in chronological order from normal drift through retrograde and back.
Match each card to both a sky-view feature and a heliocentric orbital configuration.
State in their own words why retrograde motion is apparent rather than a real reversal of Mars’s orbit.
